title: Estimates
summary: Turn users and actions into QPS and bytes within an order of magnitude.

parts.rule: Translate users and actions into queries per second and storage bytes. Prefer order-of-magnitude math: a day has about 10^5 seconds, so a million events per day is roughly ten per second on average. Apply a peak multiplier (often 2× to 10×) when the product spikes. Separate read QPS from write QPS. Storage is rows times bytes per row, then add a rough index overhead factor.
parts.why: Without numbers, every component looks equally necessary. With rough QPS you can justify a cache, a single primary, or a shard plan. Interviewers forgive arithmetic slips of 2×; they do not forgive skipping the estimate entirely and jumping to brands.
parts.example: Photo share: 50 million monthly actives, each opens the app 10 times a day and loads a feed of 20 thumbnails. Feed loads per day ≈ 50e6 × 10 = 5e8. Per second average ≈ 5e8 / 86400 ≈ 5800. Peak 5× → about 30k feed loads/sec. If each load hits cache for thumbnails but still needs one metadata query, metadata read QPS ≈ 30k at peak. Writes: assume 5% of opens upload one photo → 50e6 × 10 × 0.05 / 86400 ≈ 290 writes/sec average. Each photo metadata row 500 bytes; over two years that is on the order of several TB of metadata before replicas. You now know a single laptop DB is unlikely for peak reads, while write volume might still fit one primary with read replicas.
parts.use: Estimate before proposing caches, shards, or queues. Estimate read and write separately. Revisit the numbers when a deep dive changes the access pattern or adds a fanout multiplier.
parts.refuse: Refuse fake precision like 4837.2 QPS when the inputs were guesses. Refuse designing multi-shard pipelines before showing at least one QPS line. Refuse treating daily totals as if they were per-second loads. Refuse ignoring peak versus average when the product is bursty.

body:
Rule. Translate users and actions into queries per second and storage bytes. Prefer order-of-magnitude math: a day has about 10^5 seconds, so a million events per day is roughly ten per second on average. Apply a peak multiplier (often 2× to 10×) when the product spikes. Separate read QPS from write QPS. Storage is rows times bytes per row, then add a rough index overhead factor.

Why it matters. Without numbers, every component looks equally necessary. With rough QPS you can justify a cache, a single primary, or a shard plan. Interviewers forgive arithmetic slips of 2×; they do not forgive skipping the estimate entirely and jumping to brands.

Worked example. Photo share: 50 million monthly actives, each opens the app 10 times a day and loads a feed of 20 thumbnails. Feed loads per day ≈ 50e6 × 10 = 5e8. Per second average ≈ 5e8 / 86400 ≈ 5800. Peak 5× → about 30k feed loads/sec. If each load hits cache for thumbnails but still needs one metadata query, metadata read QPS ≈ 30k at peak. Writes: assume 5% of opens upload one photo → 50e6 × 10 × 0.05 / 86400 ≈ 290 writes/sec average. Each photo metadata row 500 bytes; over two years that is on the order of several TB of metadata before replicas. You now know a single laptop DB is unlikely for peak reads, while write volume might still fit one primary with read replicas.

[[diagram:back-of-envelope]]

When to use. Estimate before proposing caches, shards, or queues. Estimate read and write separately. Revisit the numbers when a deep dive changes the access pattern or adds a fanout multiplier.

When to refuse. Refuse fake precision like 4837.2 QPS when the inputs were guesses. Refuse designing multi-shard pipelines before showing at least one QPS line. Refuse treating daily totals as if they were per-second loads. Refuse ignoring peak versus average when the product is bursty.
